systemPrompt:
You are an expert at planning interactive 3D visualizations for textbook figures.

PRIMARY CONTEXT:
The generated figure will be embedded alongside the original in a PDF reader. It should look recognizably like the source figure — same general geometry, viewpoint, labels, and proportions — but does not need to be a pixel-perfect inline replacement. Some additional controls or layout breathing room are fine if they genuinely help the learner.

INTERACTION PALETTE — choose the interactions that best fit the concept. Pick the fewest that genuinely serve the learning goal; more is not better. In "teaches", say what the learner understands, not what the control does.

• orbit / drag — rotate/move the scene. When depth or 3D shape IS the concept.
• hover — reveal a label on demand. When showing every label at once clutters.
• click — highlight one element. When focus on one part of a busy scene matters.
• slider — sweep one continuous variable. When dragging it visibly transforms the figure.
• toggle — switch between 2+ named views. For before/after or dual views (e.g. spatial ↔ frequency).
• button / state — step through discrete phases. When distinct stages should be visited deliberately.
• animation — self-playing motion. When the concept is inherently dynamic and a slider can't convey it.
• equation_input — learner types math, parsed at runtime. When "change the formula, reshape the output" (integrand, boundary, kernel); each field maps to one curve/quantity; catch parse errors inline.
• code_editor — learner writes/debugs an algorithm; the figure replays its execution frame by frame. Use ONLY when the concept IS a procedure whose intermediate states carry the lesson — heapify, one pass of a sort, a graph traversal, gradient descent, scanline fill — i.e. the question a learner has is "in what order does it touch the data, and why". Needs state small enough to draw whole (~30 elements) and an algorithm expressible in ~20 lines against a handful of operations. Do NOT use it for a continuous parameter (that is a slider), a formula the learner retypes (equation_input), or a static structure with no execution (hover/click). Choose it over animation when the learner should be able to get the procedure WRONG and watch where it diverges.

Output ONLY valid JSON (no markdown, no explanation):
{
  "projection_type": "perspective | axonometric | oblique",
  "camera_view": { "azimuthDeg": <perspective only — 0=side · 45=three-quarter · 90=front-on>, "elevationDeg": <perspective only — 0=eye-level · 20-35=slightly above · 90=top-down>, "rollDeg": 0, "heightFraction": <0.5 default · up to 0.75 to fill the frame> },
  "axis_screen_angles": <axonometric only — null for a flat 2D plot/diagram with no 3D depth (front-on view); omit this field entirely for a 3D axonometric figure (renderer uses a standard isometric pose)>,
  "elements": ["exhaustive list of every geometric element visible in the figure that must be recreated in 3D"],
  "interactions": [
    { "id": "uniqueCamelCaseId", "type": "orbit | drag | hover | click | slider | toggle | button | state | animation | equation_input | code_editor", "teaches": "what the learner understands", "...": "plus ONLY that type's fields — see INTERACTION FIELDS below" }
  ],
  "demo_steps": [
    {
      "title": "Step name shown in UI",
      "narration": "What the learner sees and understands at this step — one or two sentences",
      "state": { "interactionId": value }
    }
  ],
  "geometry_notes": "Approximate world-space scale (e.g. 'cube ~2 units side, axes span ±3'), dominant colors from the source, and any domain-specific formula or value needed for correctness.",
  "notes": "Three.js / rendering technique notes (distinct from geometry_notes)"
}

INTERACTION FIELDS — every interaction object has "id" (unique camelCase), "type", and "teaches". Add ONLY the fields listed for its type; never attach a "range" to anything but a slider.

"type" MUST be exactly one of these 11 strings: "orbit" · "drag" · "hover" · "click" · "slider" · "toggle" · "button" · "state" · "animation" · "equation_input" · "code_editor""

• orbit / drag / hover / click — no extra fields.
• animation      — "label", optional "loop": true | false.
• slider         — "label", "range": [min, max, step], "default": <number>.
• toggle         — "label", "options": ["A", "B", ...], "default": "A"   (a plain on/off toggle may drop "options" and use "default": true | false).
• button / state — "label", "states": ["idle", "running", "done"], "default": "idle".
• equation_input — "label", "fields": [ { "id": "...", "label": "f(x) =", "default": "sin(x)", "variables": ["x"], "domain": [min, max], "role": "integrand | boundary | kernel | ..." } ]. "domain" is the x-range the field is plotted over; always supply it so the generator does not have to guess.
• code_editor    — "label",
                   "entry_point": "the one function the learner must define, e.g. buildMaxHeap(heap)",
                   "api": [ { "op": "greater(i, j)", "does": "true when A[i] > A[j]" }, { "op": "swap(i, j)", "does": "exchange two elements — the ONLY way to mutate" }, ... ],
                   "frame": "what one recorded step shows, e.g. 'the whole array plus the 1-2 indices the op touched'",
                   "input": { "label": "Initial array", "default": "4, 1, 3, 2, 16, 9, 10" },
                   "sample_code": "<correct implementation, as a string>",
                   optional "buggy_code": "<plausible near-miss, with a comment naming the bug>",
                   "success_check": "the property the final state must satisfy, e.g. 'every parent >= both of its children'".
  Design the "api" first and keep it minimal: 4–7 ops covering read, compare, mutate, and annotate (a note/mark op for the learner's own commentary). Every state change must be reachable ONLY through an op — otherwise the replay has gaps. The learner writes algorithm logic, never drawing code.

demo_steps "state" may set values for slider, toggle, and button/state interactions only; code_editor and equation_input are seeded by their sample_code / fields defaults, not by demo_steps.

Rules:
- PROJECTION TYPE: pick whichever the source most resembles. Do not measure angles off the image — the renderer applies a fixed standard pose for each type, so a coarse visual call is enough. Spend your effort on ELEMENTS and INTERACTIONS instead; camera is a quick classification, not a measurement task.
  • "perspective" — depth edges clearly converge toward a vanishing point, or a single object's own far end reads smaller than its near end. Judge within one object; a row of separate same-shape objects that merely shrink (e.g. neural-net layers) is not perspective.
  • "oblique" — one face is drawn true (an undistorted rectangle: right angles, horizontal/vertical edges intact) while depth recedes off it along a single diagonal — e.g. stacked feature maps/filter banks drawn as offset same-size copies.
  • "axonometric" — the default for everything else: any other 3D-looking figure (axes tilted, no true face), or a flat 2D plot/diagram (set "axis_screen_angles": null for these).
- CAMERA VIEW: camera_view sets framing only. azimuthDeg/elevationDeg apply to perspective only: azimuthDeg 0 side, 45 three-quarter, 90 front-on; elevationDeg 0 eye-level, 10–20 low-angle, 25–35 moderate three-quarter, 90 top-down. rollDeg is usually 0. heightFraction is how much of the frame the figure should fill (0.5 default, up to 0.75).
- DEMO STEPS: include when the concept has 2+ distinct phases the learner should visit in sequence, each step driving one named configuration of the interaction state. Use [] for a single continuous exploration with no natural sequence.
- GEOMETRY NOTES: always fill this in — it is what stops the generator guessing sizes and getting the zoom wrong. Cover:
  • world-space dimensions, and for oblique/axonometric figures give each box explicitly as X × Y × Z world units, naming which source dimension each axis carries (+X is screen-right, +Y screen-up, +Z the receding diagonal).
  • the colour palette, with hex codes where determinable from the source.
  • any formula or numeric range the generator needs to be mathematically correct.
  • POSITION AND ORIENTATION for each element as read off the source — which way it points, what angle it sits at, which side of another element it is on. Read this off the image; do not infer layout from general knowledge of the concept. A generic, plausible-looking arrangement is the failure mode the generator falls into whenever geometry_notes covers only dimensions.
  • for a repeated shape with a stated per-element value (channel count, layer size, category), an explicit number for each element's varying dimension tied to that value — equal values get equal size, even across sequence position — rather than a described trend.
- MULTI-PART FIGURES: if the source contains multiple labeled panels ((a)/(b)/(c), side-by-side comparisons, before/after pairs, sequential diagrams), do NOT recreate them all simultaneously in the initial view. Show one panel by default and link the rest through a single interaction — a toggle, tab, or slider — so the learner actively moves between parts. The transition itself should teach the comparison or progression.
- Prefer interactions that expose relationships in the figure rather than generic controls.

userContent.text:
Figure: CNX_Precalc_Figure_10_01_013

AUTHOR-PROVIDED INTERACTION REQUESTS:
Requested interactions:
- Click for an outgoing sound ray from F': the learner selects one path and its reflection point and return segment to F are highlighted, making clear that different launch angles still arrive at the other focus.
- Animation for sound propagation: the learner plays pulses leaving F', bouncing once off the ellipsoidal dome, and converging at F, making clear the dynamic reflection path behind the whispering-chamber effect.
- Toggle between single-ray and all-rays views: the learner switches from one highlighted route to the full fan of reflected paths, making clear that the focus-to-focus property is systematic rather than a coincidence of one ray.

Source file:
OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 10: Analytic Geometry

Use these requested interactions when forming the plan. Use the image to recover visual structure, layout, labels, camera/view cues, and missing visible elements.

Planner context:
This figure is a shaded three-dimensional cutaway drawing of a domed room built as a half-ellipsoid on a circular base. The outer shell carries a blue-to-white gradient and is cut away at the front so the viewer looks into the interior, where the inner surface and the floor are shaded warm tan; a thick gray band forms the base slab beneath the floor. Two small dark points on the floor mark the foci, labeled F' on the left and F on the right. A fan of dark blue segments with arrowheads leaves F', rises at a range of angles to strike the inside of the curved dome at several separated points, and reflects back down, every one arriving at F. The paths cross one another mid-room, and no two share a bounce point. Drawing many distinct routes between the same pair of labeled points emphasizes that the convergence holds no matter which direction a ray sets out in. The illustration accounts for the acoustics of a whispering chamber, where a person speaking softly at one focus of an elliptical dome is heard clearly by a listener at the other.

CONTEXT FROM TEXTBOOK:
This figure is a shaded three-dimensional cutaway drawing of a domed room built as a half-ellipsoid on a circular base. The outer shell carries a blue-to-white gradient and is cut away at the front so the viewer looks into the interior, where the inner surface and the floor are shaded warm tan; a thick gray band forms the base slab beneath the floor. Two small dark points on the floor mark the foci, labeled F' on the left and F on the right. A fan of dark blue segments with arrowheads leaves F', rises at a range of angles to strike the inside of the curved dome at several separated points, and reflects back down, every one arriving at F. The paths cross one another mid-room, and no two share a bounce point. Drawing many distinct routes between the same pair of labeled points emphasizes that the convergence holds no matter which direction a ray sets out in. The illustration accounts for the acoustics of a whispering chamber, where a person speaking softly at one focus of an elliptical dome is heard clearly by a listener at the other.

PROJECTION TYPE: perspective
Use the scaffold's true perspective projection after building all geometry. Use this only when the source has real vanishing-point convergence or distance-based size shrinkage; then depth should visibly affect apparent size.

ELEMENTS TO RECREATE IN 3D:
  - half-ellipsoid dome outer shell with blue-to-white vertical gradient, cut away across the front so the interior is visible
  - thin white/light rim strip along the cutaway edge of the shell (shell thickness)
  - inner surface of the dome shaded warm tan, visible through the cutaway
  - faint horizontal banding/highlight ring on the inner dome wall
  - elliptical floor disk of the room, warm tan gradient (lighter toward the front)
  - thick dark-gray base slab cylinder beneath the floor, slightly wider than the floor
  - focus point F' marked as a small dark dot on the floor, left side
  - focus point F marked as a small dark dot on the floor, right side
  - text label F' below-left of the left focus dot
  - text label F below-right of the right focus dot
  - fan of six dark-blue sound rays: each leaves F' at a different launch angle, strikes a distinct point on the inner dome, and returns to F
  - arrowheads placed midway along each outgoing segment and each returning segment
  - six distinct bounce points on the inner dome surface (no two rays share one)
  - crossing pattern of ray segments in the middle of the room

GEOMETRY NOTES (world-space scale, color palette, and any formula/value needed for correctness — build to these so sizes, zoom, and colors match the source; do not guess dimensions the notes already specify):
Room is the upper half (y >= 0) of a prolate spheroid with the major axis horizontal along +X (screen-right): x²/9 + y²/4 + z²/4 = 1, i.e. semi-axes a = 3 along X, b = c = 2 along Y (up) and Z (toward viewer). This ellipsoid-of-revolution form is required for the exact 3D focus-to-focus reflection property. Foci lie on the floor plane y = 0 at (±√5, 0, 0) ≈ (±2.236, 0, 0): F' at x = -2.236 (left), F at x = +2.236 (right); draw each as a dark navy dot ~0.09 radius sitting on the floor. Floor is the ellipse x²/9 + z²/4 = 1 at y = 0 (reads as a circle under the perspective view). Base slab is a matching elliptical cylinder of the same footprint scaled 1.07, extending from y = -0.45 to y = 0, dark gray #4a4a4a with a lighter top edge #8a8a8a. Shell thickness ~0.07 drawn as a white/pale rim #f2f4f6 along the cutaway edge. The cutaway removes the front of the shell roughly for z > 0 (viewer side) above y ≈ 0.55, so the eye looks through into the tan interior; the blue exterior remains as a crescent around the back and sides.
Colors: outer shell gradient from #2f7fc1 / #4a93cf at the top to near-white #eaf2f9 at the base; inner dome surface warm tan gradient #d9c79a (top) to #f2e6c6 (bottom); floor #ecdfba brightening to #f7edd4 near the front; rays and arrowheads dark navy #1c4e80 with line width ~3 px; labels F' and F in black serif italic, placed just below and slightly outside each dot.
Rays: six paths, each two straight segments F' -> P_i -> F where P_i is on the spheroid surface. Suggested bounce points (parameterize by polar angle t from +X and elevation): P1 near the left-of-center dome at (-1.4, 1.82, 0.3), P2 at (-0.2, 1.99, -0.35), P3 at (0.0, 2.0, 0.55), P4 at (1.3, 1.83, -0.5), P5 at (2.1, 1.44, 0.4), P6 at (-2.3, 1.29, -0.45) — snap each exactly onto x²/9+y²/4+z²/4=1. Arrowheads sit at ~55% along the outgoing leg (pointing up/outward) and ~55% along the return leg (pointing down toward F). Every path has the same total length 2a = 6 world units, which is why animated pulses arrive simultaneously.

DISCRETE CONTROLS (implement every one of these in #ui, each must work independently):
[
  {
    "id": "orbitDome",
    "type": "orbit",
    "teaches": "the dome is a true three-dimensional half-spheroid and the rays leave the vertical plane, yet every bounce still redirects to the same floor point"
  },
  {
    "id": "selectRay",
    "type": "click",
    "teaches": "picking any single launch direction out of F' highlights its bounce point and return leg, showing that this one arbitrary angle still lands exactly on F"
  },
  {
    "id": "rayView",
    "type": "toggle",
    "label": "Ray display",
    "options": [
      "Single ray",
      "All rays"
    ],
    "default": "Single ray",
    "teaches": "the focus-to-focus reflection is systematic: the whole fan of launch angles produces the same arrival point, not a lucky single path"
  },
  {
    "id": "soundPulse",
    "type": "animation",
    "label": "Play sound pulse from F'",
    "loop": true,
    "teaches": "sound pulses leaving F' at different angles bounce once off the dome and reconverge at F, and the equal total path lengths mean they arrive together — the whispering-chamber effect"
  }
]

DEMO STEPS (tween through these using goToStep(); each step drives the controls above):
[
  {
    "title": "One whispered ray",
    "narration": "A single sound ray leaves the left focus F', rises to the inner dome, and reflects straight down to the right focus F.",
    "state": {
      "rayView": "Single ray"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "Watch it travel",
    "narration": "Play the pulse: the wavefront climbs to the dome, turns at the bounce point, and arrives at F.",
    "state": {
      "rayView": "Single ray"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "The whole fan",
    "narration": "Switch to all rays. Six different launch angles hit six different spots on the dome, yet every one comes back to F — and all the pulses arrive at the same instant.",
    "state": {
      "rayView": "All rays"
    }
  }
]

CAMERA VIEW (framing only). Call setCameraView({ projection, ...these }) AFTER all geometry is added. Keep the projection MECHANISM from PROJECTION TYPE above (orthographic / sheared-oblique / perspective). For perspective these params set the pose (azimuth/elevation/roll); for the two parallel projections pose is a standard default (see PROJECTION TYPE above), and these params set only roll and framing (heightFraction):
{
  "azimuthDeg": 90,
  "elevationDeg": 18,
  "rollDeg": 0,
  "heightFraction": 0.62
}

NOTES: Build the dome as a scaled UV sphere (SphereGeometry, phiLength full, thetaLength PI/2 for the upper half) scaled (3,2,2); render two nested meshes — outer shell with BackSide-culled front cap removed via a clipping plane at z = +0.15 combined with y > 0.55, inner surface with THREE.BackSide and the tan gradient so the interior lights up. Use a vertex-colored or shader gradient rather than textures for the blue-to-white and tan-to-cream ramps. Soft hemisphere light plus one key directional light from upper-left; no hard shadows. Rays as TubeGeometry or Line2 (fat lines) for clean thickness; arrowheads as small ConeGeometry oriented along the segment. Highlighted ray in a brighter cyan-navy (#2f8fd8) with the others dimmed to 25% opacity. Animated pulse = small emissive sphere advancing along the polyline at constant speed with a short fading trail; when all rays are shown, launch all six pulses simultaneously so the simultaneous arrival at F is visible. Labels F' and F as CSS2D/sprite text that stays upright while orbiting. Clamp orbit elevation to 5°-70° and keep the cutaway facing the camera by rotating the clipping plane with the camera azimuth.

Follow the interaction plan above.

outputText:
Whispering chamber (elliptical dome)
Drag to orbit the dome. Click any ray in the 3D view to highlight it.
Ray display
Select launch angle from F′
Guided steps
// @FIGURE_CODE_BEGIN /* ELEMENT SPEC halo shell -> SphereGeometry(1,72,36,0,2PI,0,PI/2) scale 1.035*(3,2,2), BackSide, #f2f4f6 outer blue dome -> same sphere, scale (3,2,2), FrontSide, vertex gradient #2f7fc1 -> #eaf2f9, clipped: removed where (y < 1.0 AND near-camera half) [clipIntersection] inner tan dome -> same sphere, scale 0.985*(3,2,2), BackSide, gradient #d9c79a -> #f2e6c6 cut rim strip -> TubeGeometry elliptical ring at y=1.0 on r=1 shell, #f2f4f6 inner bands -> 2 thin elliptical TubeGeometry rings on inner wall, faint tan floor -> CircleGeometry(1,80) rot -PI/2, scale(3,2,1), gradient #ecdfba -> #f7edd4 slab -> CylinderGeometry(1,1,0.45,80) scale(3.21,1,2.14) #4a4a4a slab top rim -> RingGeometry(1.0,1.07,80) rot -PI/2 scale(3,2,1) #8a8a8a foci dots -> SphereGeometry(0.09) at (+-sqrt5,0.02,0) #16324f rays -> 6 x (2 TubeGeometry legs, radius .035) navy #1c4e80 arrowheads -> ConeGeometry(0.085,0.22) at 55% of each leg, navy pulses -> SphereGeometry(0.075) + 2 trail spheres, #7fd0ff */ renderer.localClippingEnabled = true; const CUT_Y = 1.0; const A = 3, B = 2, C = 2; // semi-axes const FX = Math.sqrt(A * A - B * B); // 2.236 const NAVY = 0x1c4e80, CYAN = 0x2f8fd8; /* ── helpers ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */ function paintGradient(geo, fn) { const pos = geo.attributes.position; const col = new Float32Array(pos.count * 3); const c = new THREE.Color(); for (let i = 0; i < pos.count; i++) { fn(pos.getX(i), pos.getY(i), pos.getZ(i), c); col[i * 3] = c.r; col[i * 3 + 1] = c.g; col[i * 3 + 2] = c.b; } geo.setAttribute('color', new THREE.BufferAttribute(col, 3)); return geo; } const CA = new THREE.Color(), CB = new THREE.Color(); function ramp(hexLo, hexHi, t, out) { CA.setHex(hexLo); CB.setHex(hexHi); out.copy(CA).lerp(CB, Math.max(0, Math.min(1, t))); } function ellipseRing(semiX, semiZ, y, tubeR, color, opacity) { const pts = []; for (let i = 0; i <= 160; i++) { const a = (i / 160) * Math.PI * 2; pts.push(new THREE.Vector3(semiX * Math.cos(a), y, semiZ * Math.sin(a))); } const curve = new THREE.CatmullRomCurve3(pts, true); const m = new THREE.Mesh( new THREE.TubeGeometry(curve, 200, tubeR, 8, true), new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color, transparent: opacity < 1, opacity }) ); return m; } /* ── dome shells ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */ const domeGeoSrc = () => new THREE.SphereGeometry(1, 72, 36, 0, Math.PI * 2, 0, Math.PI / 2); // halo (shell thickness seen at the silhouette) const halo = new THREE.Mesh( domeGeoSrc(), new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0xf2f4f6, side: THREE.BackSide }) ); halo.scale.set(A * 1.035, B * 1.035, C * 1.035); scene.add(halo); // outer blue shell, cut away toward the viewer below CUT_Y const planeTop = new THREE.Plane(new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0), -CUT_Y / B); // local space? -> world below planeTop.constant = -CUT_Y; const planeFar = new THREE.Plane(new THREE.Vector3(0, 0, 1), 0); const outerGeo = paintGradient(domeGeoSrc(), (x, y, z, c) => { ramp(0xeaf2f9, 0x2f7fc1, Math.pow(Math.max(0, y), 0.75), c); }); const outerMat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ vertexColors: true, side: THREE.FrontSide, clippingPlanes: [planeTop, planeFar], clipIntersection: true }); const outer = new THREE.Mesh(outerGeo, outerMat); outer.scale.set(A, B, C); scene.add(outer); // inner tan surface (back side => we see the far interior wall) const innerGeo = paintGradient(domeGeoSrc(), (x, y, z, c) => { ramp(0xf2e6c6, 0xd9c79a, Math.pow(Math.max(0, y), 0.7), c); }); const inner = new THREE.Mesh(innerGeo, new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ vertexColors: true, side: THREE.BackSide })); inner.scale.set(A * 0.985, B * 0.985, C * 0.985); scene.add(inner); // white rim strip along the cut edge (only the front arc is unoccluded) { const f = Math.sqrt(1 - (CUT_Y / B) * (CUT_Y / B)); scene.add(ellipseRing(A * f, C * f, CUT_Y, 0.05, 0xf2f4f6, 1)); } // faint banding on the inner wall [[0.52, 0xcdb98c, 0.55], [0.88, 0xe6d6ab, 0.45]].forEach(([yy, col, op]) => { const k = 0.982; const f = Math.sqrt(Math.max(0.001, 1 - (yy / (B * k)) * (yy / (B * k)))); scene.add(ellipseRing(A * k * f, C * k * f, yy, 0.018, col, op)); }); /* ── floor + base slab ───────────────────────────────────────────────── */ const floorGeo = paintGradient(new THREE.CircleGeometry(1, 80), (x, y, z, c) => { ramp(0xecdfba, 0xf7edd4, (-y + 1) / 2, c); // local +y -> world -z (back) }); const floor = new THREE.Mesh(floorGeo, new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ vertexColors: true, side: THREE.DoubleSide })); floor.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; floor.scale.set(A, C, 1); scene.add(floor); const slabGeo = paintGradient(new THREE.CylinderGeometry(1, 1, 0.45, 80, 1, false), (x, y, z, c) => { ramp(0x3a3a3a, 0x565656, (y + 0.225) / 0.45, c); }); const slab = new THREE.Mesh(slabGeo, new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ vertexColors: true })); slab.position.y = -0.225; slab.scale.set(A * 1.07, 1, C * 1.07); scene.add(slab); const rim = new THREE.Mesh( new THREE.RingGeometry(1.0, 1.07, 80), new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x8a8a8a, side: THREE.DoubleSide }) ); rim.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2; rim.position.y = 0.003; rim.scale.set(A, C, 1); scene.add(rim); /* ── foci ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */ const Fp = new THREE.Vector3(-FX, 0.02, 0); const Fr = new THREE.Vector3(FX, 0.02, 0); const dotMat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x16324f, depthTest: false }); [Fp, Fr].forEach(p => { const m = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.SphereGeometry(0.09, 20, 14), dotMat); m.position.copy(p); m.renderOrder = 12; scene.add(m); }); /* ── rays ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */ const rawBounce = [ [-1.4, 1.82, 0.3], [-0.2, 1.99, -0.35], [0.0, 2.0, 0.55], [1.3, 1.83, -0.5], [2.1, 1.44, 0.4], [-2.3, 1.29, -0.45] ]; function snap(p) { const u = new THREE.Vector3(p[0] / A, p[1] / B, p[2] / C).normalize(); return new THREE.Vector3(u.x * A, Math.abs(u.y) * B, u.z * C); } const bounce = rawBounce.map(snap); function legMesh(a, b, mat) { return new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.TubeGeometry(new THREE.LineCurve3(a, b), 1, 0.035, 10, false), mat); } function arrowMesh(a, b, mat) { const dir = new THREE.Vector3().subVectors(b, a).normalize(); const cone = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.ConeGeometry(0.085, 0.24, 14), mat); cone.position.copy(a).lerp(b, 0.55); cone.quaternion.setFromUnitVectors(new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0), dir); return cone; } const rays = []; bounce.forEach((P, i) => { const mat = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: NAVY, depthTest: false, transparent: false, opacity: 1 }); const g = new THREE.Group(); const parts = [legMesh(Fp, P, mat), legMesh(P, Fr, mat), arrowMesh(Fp, P, mat), arrowMesh(P, Fr, mat)]; parts.forEach(m => { m.renderOrder = 10; g.add(m); }); scene.add(g); const L1 = Fp.distanceTo(P), L2 = P.distanceTo(Fr); // pulse + trail const pulseMats = []; const pulses = []; for (let k = 0; k < 3; k++) { const pm = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: 0x7fd0ff, depthTest: false, transparent: true, opacity: 1 - k * 0.33 }); systemPrompt:
You are a strict critic of generated interactive Three.js 3D figures against original 2D textbook figure images.
You will receive the original source figure image, the generated HTML/JavaScript code, and a rendered screenshot of the generated HTML (if screenshot capture succeeds). Start by using the screenshot to help evaluate the faithfulness of the generated figure to the source figure, listing discrepancies in the primitive elements between what you see in the source figure versus what you see in the generated figure. If the screenshot was not received, mention this in the notes.
Score the generated figure using the rubric and give feedback to improve the figure. Be critical and honest — err toward lower scores when in doubt. Ensure that the output is not a 2D image rendered with Three.js. Do not give credit for things that are absent or barely present. Output ONLY a valid JSON object — no explanation, no markdown, no fences.

AUTOMATED VERIFICATION ALREADY PASSED. A deterministic verifier has rendered this figure headless at multiple viewports and confirmed it runs without exceptions or console errors with the render loop alive, actually draws to the GPU (non-blank canvas, real geometry, no NaN coordinates), fits the viewport with no overflow and the control panel fully on-screen, and has labels that are on-screen, not enormous, and not heavily overlapping.
Spend NO scores, failure modes, discrepancies, or action items on any of that. Focus ENTIRELY on SEMANTIC FIDELITY to the source: correct geometry, correct primitives, correct camera/view, faithful composition and colors, correct and meaningful labels, meaningful and conceptually-correct interactions, and concept accuracy. Judge whether it is the *right* figure and a good teaching artifact — not whether it renders.

SCAFFOLD CONTEXT (provided automatically — do not penalise for missing these):
- THREE, OrbitControls, renderer, scene, orthographic camera, controls, animate loop, ResizeObserver are all pre-wired
- addLabel(text, position3D, {color, fontSize, bold, offset, background}?) — floating HTML label system
- setStandardView({azimuth, polar, heightFraction}?) — frames the camera to scene content
- Reset View is scaffolded; generated code may add controls, panels, and UI affordances as needed to support the planned interactions

DISCREPANCIES - list 0-6 visual discrepancies between the source figure and the generated figure, prioritized by impact on recognizability and concept accuracy
- Focus on: wrong geometric primitives, missing or incorrect elements, wrong colors, missing or mislabeled annotations, broken or absent interactions
- De-prioritize: minor camera angle differences, exact crop/zoom, whitespace variation — only flag these if they make the figure hard to recognize or misleading
- For multipanel source figures, if the generated figure implements a toggle/tab/step between parts (e.g. Part A vs Part B), check the HTML/JS before flagging a part as "missing" — a part hidden behind an unactivated toggle is not a discrepancy

FAILURE MODES — list any that apply (use empty array [] if none):
"Depth-Wrong"             — 3D depth/perspective interpretation is incorrect
"Missing-Labels"          — important text annotations are absent
"Wrong-Primitives"        — incorrect geometric shapes used for the concept
"Interaction-Broken"      — interactive controls are present but non-functional
"Interaction-Missing"     — no meaningful interactions beyond basic OrbitControls rotation
"Camera-Wrong"            — initial viewpoint differs from the source figure — wrong angle/orientation/rotation, even if all content remains visible
"Scale-Wrong"             — element proportions are noticeably off
"Color-Wrong"             — colors don't match the original figure
"Hallucination"           — elements present that do not appear in the original
"Concept-Misunderstood"   — the core concept being illustrated is    misrepresented

SCORES — integer 1–5 for each field:
geometry_accuracy — Judge these five things:
  • CAMERA — flag "Camera-Wrong" only if the vantage point differs enough to make the figure hard to recognize (reversed foreground/background, a key face hidden, viewed from the opposite side). Minor azimuth/zoom differences do not qualify.
  • PRIMITIVES — flag "Wrong-Primitives" and cap the score when a major element uses the wrong shape (a box drawn as a cone/pyramid, a plane as a disc, a ray as a thick cylinder), even if the composition looks similar.
  • PROJECTION MECHANISM — axonometric = off-axis orthographic, no shear; oblique = front-on orthographic plus a consistent depth shear; perspective = true perspective, used when the source shows convergence or distance-based shrinking.
  • REPEATED ELEMENTS — compare each corresponding element's size and proportions to the source, not just its presence. A set that should visibly vary in size but came out uniform is a spatial error, even if each element is individually a plausible primitive.
  • HARD FLOOR — if the source has genuine 3D structure (elements at different depths, occlusion, a meaningfully three-dimensional arrangement) but the generated figure flattened it into a camera-facing poster with no occlusion or depth falloff, score geometry_accuracy 1 and include "Depth-Wrong", regardless of how correct the colors/labels/elements are. Does NOT apply when the source is itself a flat 2D diagram the plan correctly renders front-on (axis_screen_angles: null).
  5 – All elements represented; plausible positions, connections, proportions
  4 – All major elements present; minor position/alignment issues
  3 – 1-2 elements missing OR noticeable spatial errors; concept still recognizable
  2 – Multiple missing elements OR major spatial errors
  1 – Unrecognizable or completely wrong topology

interactivity_usability — CRITICAL: OrbitControls (mouse drag to rotate/zoom) does NOT count as an interaction. Meaningful interactions = buttons, sliders, toggles, step-through animations, parameter controls built by the developer.
  5 – All planned interactions functional and pedagogically useful; count matches figure complexity (1 deep slider is correct for a single-variable concept; 3+ expected for multi-step figures); demo steps present if the plan includes them
  4 – Most planned interactions functional; minor usability issues; pedagogical value clear
  3 – At least one meaningful interaction works; some planned interactions missing or broken; or interactions only weakly connected to the concept
  2 – Interactions exist in code but broken or no visible effect
  1 – Only OrbitControls present, or no interactions at all — score MUST be 1

faithfulness — Judge overall visual resemblance to the source — composition, geometry, and color scheme at a glance — rather than an exhaustive checklist of small differences. For multipanel source figures where the generated figure implements a toggle/tab/step between parts (e.g. Part A vs Part B), it is correct and expected for only one part to be visible in the default screenshot; check the HTML/JS for a toggle control before penalizing a currently-hidden part as missing or absent. Do not over-penalize extra elements added beyond the source (additional UI chrome, decorative touches) unless they clutter the figure or change its overall look — flag those under the Hallucination failure mode rather than cutting this score for minor additions.
  5 – Clearly recognizable as the same figure: correct geometry, colors, composition, and major labels all present
  4 – Recognizable at a glance; minor differences in color, proportion, or label placement
  3 – General idea clear but notable differences in geometry, composition, or missing elements
  2 – Hard to recognize as the same figure; significant content differences
  1 – Completely different or fabricated

label_quality — Off-screen / heavily-overlapping labels are already caught by the verifier — do not re-flag those. Judge CONTENT (right labels present, correct text, on the correct element, matching the source) and LEGIBILITY (comfortably readable even when the verifier did not call them "enormous", with a deliberate hierarchy — primary labels standing out over axis labels — matching what the source implies).
  5 – All the right labels present, correct text on the correct elements, matching the source, AND sized/styled for easy legibility with a clear hierarchy matching the source
  4 – Content correct; only 1-2 minor issues (content OR sizing/hierarchy — e.g. a label slightly too small or inconsistently sized)
  3 – Half of labels have issues, whether content (wrong text, wrong target, missing, unclear) or legibility (uncomfortably small, inconsistent hierarchy)
  2 – Most labels problematic — mislabeled/missing content, or generally too small/cluttered to read comfortably
  1 – No labels, or all wrong/mislabeled/illegible

concept_accuracy:
  5 – All concepts accurate; interactions demonstrate correct relationships; no misinformation
  4 – Main concept correct; ≤1 minor detail wrong or missing
  3 – Main concept present; 2-3 details wrong or missing
  2 – Significant errors or fabrications; would mislead students
  1 – Completely incorrect or misleading

ACTION ITEMS — separate feedback for the generation and the plan:
- action_items: list 2-4 generation-level fixes (broken controls, wrong primitives, missing labels, scale issues, camera/view correction — things fixable without changing the plan)
- plan_action_items: list 0-2 plan-level fixes (wrong projection_type, missing core elements, wrong interaction type for the concept, fundamental misunderstanding — things requiring a revised plan). Use [] if the plan is sound.

Output this exact JSON structure and nothing else:
{
  "discrepancies": [],
  "failure_modes": [],
  "geometry_accuracy": 3,
  "interactivity_usability": 3,
  "faithfulness": 3,
  "label_quality": 3,
  "concept_accuracy": 3,
  "notes": "one concise sentence summarizing the main strengths and weaknesses",
  "action_items": [
    "Specific generation-level fix 1",
    "Specific generation-level fix 2"
  ],
  "plan_action_items": [
    "Specific plan-level fix 1 (or empty array if plan is sound)"
  ]
}
